newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian farmers snub PM, Horn says talks over.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian farmers snub PM, Horn says talks over.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn declared talks with protesting farmers were at an end on Wednesday after they snubbed him by failing to show up at a meeting.
"The government regards the talks as finished," Horn told reporters.
He said the government did not want to conduct further talks on tax regulations or social security contributions with the farmers, whose protests have included blocking highways throughout Hungary.
The farmers from the central Kiskoros region started roadblocks on February 24 protesting that taxes were too high and demanding that they be exempt from making social security contributions.
Last Tuesday the government accepted the majority of their claims and promised to amend regulations.

However, Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy, who wrote the agreement letter on the government's behalf, told journalists that regular employees still pay twice as much tax as farmers do and that he would not agree to regulations that would result in unequal burdens.
"I am unwilling to agree to any substantial change affecting the proportionate sharing of tax burdens," Medgyessy said.
On Tuesday Horn told parliament that in 1995, only 13,000 out of Hungary's 1.5 million farmers submitted an income tax return.
Last Friday Kiskoros protesters formed an association, MTESZ, and demanded further talks with government officials.

On Monday Medgyessy refused to attend talks with MTESZ in Kiskoros, but invited them, along with other farmers' associations, to attend a meeting on Wednesday with finance and agriculture ministry officials.
He was, however, convinced by Horn to meet MTESZ representatives in Budapest, together with Horn and Agriculture Minister Frigyes Nagy.
"The Kiskoros people were invited by the Prime Minister and I cannot afford to turn down an invitation from him," Medgyessy said.
MTESZ representatives, apparently dissatisfied with the talks at the Finance Ministry, cancelled their meeting with Horn. The farmers could not be reached for comment.

Peter Csobanczy, deputy state secretary at the Finance Ministry, told journalists after the talks that the meeting had been successful from the government's point of view and that they would continue the amendments as planned.
He added that the different farmers' organisations often voiced contradicting claims during the talks.
